terms.grammar: verb, first conjugation; intransitive, or with what is shouted
evidence: Plaut. Men. 1114b: Quid clāmās? quīn tacēs?
Ter. Ad. 728: Nōn clāmās? nōn īnsānis?
terms.comment: The everyday word, of people, and in comedy even of snoring; also of geese and crickets (Lewis & Short). With an object it is to call out something, or call on someone: clāmāre aliquem.

evidence: Plaut. Bacch. 874: ut nē clāmōrem hīc faciās
terms.comment: A shout or the noise of shouting: clāmōrem facere, to shout, make a row.

evidence: Cic. Tusc. 2.56 (Lewis & Short): in stadiō cursōrēs exclāmant quam maximē possunt
terms.comment: A single cry, or a sudden remark; also of a crowd applauding (Lewis & Short).
Loud, often angry shouting, as of a man raising an outcry.

phrases.english: What are you shouting for? Why don’t you keep quiet?

phrases.latin: Sciō tē bonā esse vōce, nē clāmā nimis.
phrases.english: I know you have a good voice; don’t shout so much.

phrases.latin: Nē clāmā: petītō hāsce ā mē decem.
phrases.english: Don’t shout: ask me for these ten.

sources: Lewis & Short: clamo · Lewis & Short: clamor · Lewis & Short: exclamo · Lewis & Short: vociferor
